planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in average to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this vigorous hybrid clumps up and spreads steadily, so allow room or plan on occasional division.

directions: Rebecca Moss bears soft near-white flowers that age to a deeper dusky pink, held above mounds of deeply five-lobed mid-green foliage from late spring through summer. Bred by English hardy-geranium specialist Robin Moss and named for his daughter, it is one of the toughest and most floriferous of the oxonianum hybrids, tolerating heat, drought, and poor soil once established. Shear the clump back hard after the first flush to tidy the foliage and encourage a strong rebloom into fall. It spreads readily by rhizome and self-seeds modestly, making it a reliable groundcover or border filler.

planting.note: Plant in lean, well-drained, even dry soil in full sun to light shade; this renardii hybrid resents soggy winter conditions and performs best where drainage is sharp.

directions: A cross between Geranium renardii and G. platypetalum selected by Ivan Louette in Chaumont-Gistoux, Belgium, Terre Franche forms a tidy mound of soft, velvety grey-green leaves topped from late spring into summer with lavender-blue flowers etched with darker purple veining. It is exceptionally drought tolerant once rooted in, thriving in poor, gritty soils that would make lusher cranesbills sulk, and the felted foliage stays attractive through the season. Use it along a hot, dry border edge or in a gravel garden where its understated color and texture read well against bolder neighbors. Deadhead spent flower stems to keep the mound neat and to encourage a modest second flush.

planting.note: Plant in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun to light shade; this chance garden hybrid struggles in humid, hot-summer climates and is best suited to mild, dry-summer regions.

directions: Stanhoe is a chance garden hybrid of Geranium traversii var. elegans and G. sessiliflorum var. novae-zelandiae that arose in a garden in the village of Stanhoe, Norfolk, England, and was confirmed by Cambridge University Botanic Garden's Dr. Peter Yeo. It forms a low, spreading carpet of small, rounded, silvery grey-green leaves. Pale pink flowers appear through summer, with intermittent rebloom where summers stay cool and dry. It makes an excellent groundcover for rock gardens or path edges in Mediterranean-style climates but dislikes humid heat and wet winters, where it is best treated as short-lived. Trim lightly after flowering to maintain a dense, tidy mat.

planting.note: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; low, sprawling stems appreciate being allowed to scramble through nearby perennials or over a wall.

directions: A long-cultivated selection raised by E. C. Buxton in Betws-y-Coed, Wales, this geranium bears spode-blue, white-centered flowers with darker veining and contrasting purple stamens from June through October. Its low, trailing habit works well scrambling through border neighbors, tumbling over a low wall, or carpeting the front of a bed. It is the confirmed seed parent of the famous Geranium 'Rozanne' (crossed with G. himalayense), and shares that cultivar's extended bloom season, though in a more restrained, lower-growing form. Established plants tolerate light shade well and need little more than an annual tidy-up in late winter.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; cutting the plant back hard after its first flowering flush renews the foliage color and promotes a second bloom.

directions: Dark Reiter is grown chiefly for its deeply dissected, plum-purple foliage, a dramatic foil for the clusters of lilac-blue flowers it produces from early to late summer. Slower growing and more compact than the wild meadow cranesbill, it suits the front of a border or a rock garden where its dark coloring can be appreciated up close. Shearing the mound after the first bloom cycle tidies the plant, intensifies new foliage color, and often triggers a fall rebloom. It prefers acidic, well-drained soil and resents prolonged wet conditions.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; deadhead after the first flush to encourage a later-summer rebloom.

directions: Bred by Scottish hardy-geranium specialist Alan Bremner from Geranium libani and G. ibericum subsp. jubatum, Sabani Blue forms a tight mound of finely cut foliage topped with upward-facing, vivid true-blue flowers veined in violet around a clean white eye. It flowers earlier than most hardy geraniums, typically from mid-spring into early summer, with a second flush often following in late summer if deadheaded. Its compact, drought-tolerant habit suits border edges, containers, and rock gardens, and it holds up well to full sun. Divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this low, trailing selection is well suited to containers, troughs, and rock garden pockets.

directions: Pink Spice is a low, spreading evergreen cranesbill with lobed, toothed foliage strongly flushed bronze-purple, setting off small rose-pink flowers with paler margins in early summer and often again in late summer. It arose as a chance seedling from open pollination of Geranium traversii var. elegans and G. sessiliflorum at a nursery in Tauranga, New Zealand, and is protected under plant breeders' rights. Its trailing habit and colorful foliage make it a good choice for edging, troughs, or the front of a rock garden in mild, dry-summer climates. It is less reliably hardy than most Geranium cultivars and benefits from winter protection outside its comfort zone.

planting.note: Plant in fertile, consistently moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; good air circulation helps this disease-resistant selection stay mildew-free.

directions: Natascha produces tall, conical flower clusters of rose-pink petals striped lengthwise with white, giving each bloom a distinctive pinwheel pattern reminiscent of peppermint candy, from early to midsummer. It was discovered in 1989 as a sport of Phlox maculata 'Omega' by Dutch breeder Luc Klinkhamer while visiting the Minsk Botanic Garden, and named for its curator, Natascha Lunina. Among the meadow phlox selections it stands out for excellent powdery mildew resistance, making it a dependable choice for borders, cottage gardens, and pollinator plantings. Deadheading spent flower heads encourages a tidier appearance and can prolong the display.

planting.note: Plant in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; this evergreen groundcover is drought tolerant once established and resents poorly drained winter soil.

directions: Emerald Cushion Blue forms a dense, needle-leaved evergreen mat that disappears under a sheet of deep blue flowers for several weeks in mid-spring. The tight, moss-like foliage stays attractive year-round and makes a durable groundcover for rock gardens, slopes, and wall tops. It is markedly cold hardy and shrugs off drought once rooted in, needing only a light shearing after bloom to keep the mat dense and encourage fresh growth. Give it full sun and sharp drainage, since soggy soil in winter is its main liability.
sources: New England Wild Flower Society Plant Finder

planting.note: Plant in fertile, medium-moisture, well-drained soil in full sun to part shade; good spacing and air movement help preserve this cultivar's strong mildew resistance.

directions: Little Boy is a compact garden phlox that stays well under a foot and a half tall, forming tidy upright clumps topped by large, pyramidal clusters of fragrant lilac-blue, star-shaped flowers with white eyes from mid to late summer. Its dwarf stature means the sturdy stems rarely need staking, and the plant fits neatly near the front of a border where taller phlox would overwhelm. It shows notably good resistance to powdery mildew compared with many garden phlox, and its flowers draw butterflies and hummingbirds. Divide congested clumps every few years in early spring to maintain vigorous bloom.
